---
title: "From Assistant to Agent"
subtitle: "How software around a model turns text generation into inspecting files, running code, and carrying a task through many steps"
---

*Prerequisites: the distinction between a model's parameters and its
inference-time context, from `learn/tokens-context.qmd` and
`learn/posttraining.qmd`. Both are linked where they matter; neither is
assumed.*

## 1. What a bare model call cannot do

A call to a language model maps the supplied context, the instructions,
the conversation, and whatever else was placed in the window, to
generated output. That is the whole transaction. By itself, generating
the sentence "I searched the web and found the report" does not mean a
web search happened; generating "I have fixed the bug in `parse.py`"
does not mean the file changed; generating "the tests now pass" does not
mean any test ran. A bare model call can produce text or structured
output, but by itself it does not change an external file, run a
program, search the web, or send a message. Those effects require
surrounding software, or a provider-operated tool, to execute an action.
A model can therefore produce fluent text describing actions without any
of those actions occurring.

For a system to act on files, programs, databases, or the web, software
around the model has to expose those capabilities as tools and carry out
the actions the model requests, within whatever limits the software
enforces. Everything on this page follows from keeping two things
separate: the model, which produces output from context, and the
software loop around it, which decides what enters the context, executes
what the model requests, and decides when to stop.

## 2. What actually happens in a tool call

Take one tool call literally. The surrounding software first gives the
model, as part of its inference-time context, a description of each
available tool: a name, a statement of what it does, and a schema for
the inputs it takes. Given the user's task and the rest of the context,
the model may then generate a structured request naming a tool and
supplying inputs, instead of, or in addition to, ordinary text. The
software reads that request, checks it against its permission rules and
policies, and, if allowed, runs the tool. The tool returns a result: a
file's contents, a command's output, a search's hits, an error message.
The software places that result into the context of a later model call,
and the model generates its next output using the new evidence, which
may be another tool request, a question to the user, or a final answer.

At the model boundary, then, a tool call is generated structured output.
Surrounding system infrastructure interprets that request, executes or
routes the action, and supplies the result to a subsequent model step.
The model does not open a file, run a program, or send a message by
generating text about doing so; it produces a request, and something
else acts. Which "something else" varies: often the developer's own
application, sometimes infrastructure operated by the model provider. As
one concrete, product-specific illustration: Anthropic's
API documentation, accessed 2026-09-15, describes tool use as the model
deciding when to call a tool based on the user's request and the tool's
description, then returning a structured call that the developer's own
application executes (or, for a small set of server-side tools, that
Anthropic's infrastructure executes), with the developer's code sending
the result back for the model's next turn. [S-51] Other providers'
interfaces differ in detail; the division of labor is the same.

## 3. One sustained example

Suppose a user tells a coding system:

> "Find why this script fails and fix it."

A capable system might proceed as follows. The labels in brackets say
which kind of step each one is.

1. The model, reading the task and a description of the repository's
   tools, requests a listing of the project directory. [model decision]
2. The software runs the listing and returns the file names. [tool
   execution; evidence returned]
3. The model requests that the failing script be run. [model decision]
4. The software runs it, possibly after asking the user, since running
   code can have effects, and returns the error message and traceback.
   [permission; tool execution; evidence returned]
5. The model reads the traceback, which names a function in one file,
   and requests that file's contents. [model decision]
6. The software returns the file. [tool execution; evidence returned]
7. The model proposes a bounded edit to the function and requests that
   it be applied. [model decision]
8. The software shows the proposed change and asks the user to approve
   it, then applies it. [permission; tool execution]
9. The model requests that the tests be run. [model decision]
10. The software runs them and returns the output. [tool execution;
    evidence returned]
11. If a test failed, the model continues from step 5 with the new
    evidence. If the specified checks passed, it reports what it did and
    stops. If the situation is ambiguous, for instance two plausible
    causes, it asks the user. [model decision; stopping condition]

Every "model decision" is a generated output. Every "tool execution" is
the software acting. Every "evidence returned" is new content placed in
the context for the next call. The permission steps are where the
software's rules, not the model's inclinations, determine whether an
action happens. Nothing in this sequence is specific to any product;
§11 returns to it with a concrete one.

## 4. Workflow versus agent

The word "agent" has no universally fixed definition, and this page
uses it as a useful distinction rather than a natural kind. One
vocabulary that has proved useful comes from an engineering article
Anthropic published in December 2024, which separates two kinds of
system. A [**workflow**](../glossary.qmd#workflow) is a system in which "LLMs and tools are
orchestrated through predefined code paths": the sequence of model calls
and tool uses is substantially written in advance by a programmer. An
[**agent**](../glossary.qmd#agent) is a system in which "LLMs dynamically direct their own
processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish
tasks": the model has meaningful say over which steps and tools to use
and in what order, within constraints, in pursuit of an objective.
[S-50]

A workflow example: classify an incoming document, retrieve the three
most relevant reference documents, summarize the document against them.
The path is fixed; the model fills in each step. The example in §3 is an
agent in this vocabulary: the software did not prescribe "list, run,
read, edit, test"; the model chose those steps from the evidence as it
arrived.

Neither term implies the absence of human oversight, and neither is
better in general. The same article recommends finding the simplest
solution possible and increasing complexity only when needed, and notes
that agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task
performance. [S-50] Stated as a design principle: use the simplest
system that reliably solves the task. If a fixed workflow already solves
the task reliably, giving the model more control may add cost, latency,
and failure modes without providing enough additional benefit to justify
the complexity.

## 5. The agent loop

The system in §3 is an instance of one loop, which is the minimal
mechanism behind the definition of an agent used on this page:

{{< include ../_includes/_agent-loop.qmd >}}

Read it from the top. The software assembles a context from the
objective and the current state and calls the model. The model's output
is either a structured tool request or a response. A tool request goes
through the software's permission and validation rules. If it passes,
the software executes the action against the external world and
receives an observation. The observation is added to the context, the
state is updated, and the software calls the model again. On each pass
the model may continue, ask the user, or stop; the software may also
stop it, on a step limit, a rule, or a user interruption.

One point about this loop is easy to miss. The model does not remain
running between calls, deliberating in the background. The loop advances
through distinct model steps, and continuity between those steps is
supplied by context and state that the surrounding system maintains or
supplies; how a given API or product manages that state, and what it
caches, varies. The conceptual point is that continuity belongs to the
system's context and state machinery, not to a model continuously
deliberating between calls. [S-56]

## 6. What makes agentic work possible

The loop needs a small number of ingredients, and agentic capability
comes from their combination, not from a new kind of neural network. An
"agent" is not an architecture; the model inside is the same transformer
the earlier pages describe. [S-56]

An **objective** is the task, stated well enough that progress and
completion can be recognized. The **model** produces each next action
from context. The **context** is what the model can see on a given
call: the objective, instructions, the history of actions and
observations, and any supplied material, subject to the finite window
`learn/tokens-context.qmd` describes. [**Tools**](../glossary.qmd#tool) are the capabilities the
software exposes, each with a description the model reads and an
implementation the software runs. [**External state**](../glossary.qmd#external-state) is the world the
tools act on and observe: files, a repository, a database, a web page.
A **stopping condition** says when the loop ends, whether a check
passed, a step budget ran out, or the user was asked. [**Permissions**](../glossary.qmd#permissions)
decide which requested actions are executed automatically, which need
approval, and which are refused. [**Verification**](../glossary.qmd#verification) is the use of tools to
make success observable rather than asserted, which §9 takes up. Remove
any one of these and the loop degrades in a predictable way: no
objective and it wanders, no tools and it can only talk, no stopping
condition and it does not end, no verification and its reports are
unchecked claims.

## 7. State and memory

Three kinds of state are involved, and they are easy to run together.
The model's **parameters** are fixed throughout the loop; nothing the
agent does during a task changes them. The **context window** is the
model's working input for one call, finite and reassembled every call.
**External state** is everything the software or the tools persist
outside the model: files the agent writes, a repository it commits to,
database rows it inserts, notes it saves, summaries the software stores
when the context grows too long. [S-31]

External state can be brought back into a later context, in this task
or a future one, by reading the file, querying the database, or having
the software supply the saved summary. That is retrieval into context,
and it is the mechanism behind every kind of persistence an agent
system offers. The word "memory" is used for several of these things,
and it should be qualified when it is used: system-level persistent
memory is external state that software stores and re-supplies, and it
is a different object from the model's weights (which training changes)
and from the current context (which lasts one call). An agent that
"remembers" a project across sessions has been given, by its software, a
file or store that is read back in. The behavior can change when that
state is supplied again, but no model parameter was updated.

## 8. Skills, instructions, and reusable procedures

A system can give the model reusable instructions, procedures, examples,
or resources that say how to carry out a class of tasks: how this
project's tests are run, what a good commit message looks like here,
which checks to perform before reporting a number. These are loaded into
inference-time context when relevant, and they are the natural way to
make an agent competent at a recurring task without retraining anything.
The durable concept is that reusable procedural context is not model
retraining: a procedure loaded into context changes what the model
conditions on for this task and leaves its parameters exactly as they
were. [S-31]

Claude Code, Anthropic's coding tool, is one product-specific example of
this pattern, as documented on 2026-09-15. A project can carry a
`CLAUDE.md` file of persistent instructions that the tool reads at the
start of every session, and it can define [**skills**](../glossary.qmd#skill), each a folder
with a `SKILL.md` file of instructions and optionally scripts and
resources. The documentation states that in a regular session skill
descriptions are loaded into context so the model knows what is
available, while a skill's full content is loaded only when it is
invoked, and that where a skill is saved decides which sessions load it.
[S-52] [S-53] Both are files read into context. Neither trains the
model.

## 9. Verification is part of the loop

When an agent reports "Done", that report is generated output like any
other, and it is not evidence that the task succeeded. What tools make
possible is turning success into something observable. Running the tests
shows whether the tests pass. Rendering the document shows whether it
renders. Recomputing a number in a separate script shows whether the
committed figure matches. Inspecting the version-control diff shows
exactly what changed. Querying the database shows what is actually
stored. Reading the downloaded file shows what was actually retrieved.
The engineering article cited in §4 makes the same point in its own
terms: during execution, agents need to gain "ground truth" from the
environment at each step, such as tool call results or code execution,
to assess their progress. [S-50]

The limit of verification has to be stated as carefully as its value. A
passing test provides evidence that the specified checks passed. It does
not establish that the specification, research design, or resulting
number is correct. A test checks what it was written to check, no more;
an agent that satisfies every automated check can still have solved the
wrong problem, or solved the right one in a way the checks did not
examine. For high-stakes or judgment-heavy work, human review of what
was done, not only of whether the checks passed, remains part of the
loop.

## 10. Permissions and human control

Because the software executes what the model requests, the software is
also where boundaries belong. Depending on the task and the setting, an
agent system may allow read-only actions to run automatically, require
approval before files are changed, block particular commands, restrict
what the agent may send outside the machine, limit which tools are
available at all, and impose stopping conditions. These are system-level
controls, implemented in the loop, and they hold regardless of what the
model generates. They are not properties the model acquired through
post-training, and a well-behaved model is not a substitute for them:
the article in §4 notes that the autonomy of agents brings higher costs
and the potential for compounding errors, and recommends sandboxed
testing with appropriate guardrails. [S-50]

Claude Code's permission system, as documented on 2026-09-15, is one
concrete instance. It is described as tiered. In its Manual mode, the
default approval pattern is that file reads within the allowed working
directories need no approval, shell commands require approval except for
a built-in set of read-only commands, and file modifications require
approval; explicit deny rules can prevent a tool from being used at all.
Claude Code also provides other permission modes that change which
actions require a prompt, such as a plan mode that restricts a session to
read-only exploration. [S-54] The specifics will change; the shape, in
which approval is decided by the software according to rules the user
controls, is what to take from it. Permissions are enforced by the
surrounding software, not by the model.

## 11. From assistant to coding agent

A chat assistant, as `learn/posttraining.qmd` §9 describes it, is a
post-trained model plus instructions, conversation state, and product
logic, responding turn by turn. A coding agent is the same kind of
system given more: access to a repository; tools that read and edit
files; a shell in which to run commands, tests, and builds;
version-control information; persistent project instructions of the
kind §8 describes; and the loop of §5 to hold it all together. With
those, a single request becomes a sequence:

```
inspect → plan → edit → run → observe → revise → verify → stop
```

which is the sequence the example in §3 followed.

Claude Code is one current example of such a system. Its own
documentation, accessed 2026-09-15, describes it as an agentic coding
tool that reads a codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates
with development tools, working from the terminal, an editor, or a
browser; it works with git, staging changes and creating branches and
pull requests; and it reads a project's `CLAUDE.md` at the start of
every session. [S-52] Each of those capabilities is a tool or a piece of
context in the sense of this page: the model requests a file edit or a
command, the tool runs it under the permission rules of §10, and the
result comes back as evidence. Later pages cover using it in practice;
nothing more about the product is needed to understand what it is.

## 12. Why agents fail

Agent systems fail in ways that follow directly from the loop, and it is
worth naming the common ones without pretending the list is complete.
The objective may be ambiguous, so the model pursues a reasonable
reading that was not the intended one. The context may lack something
the task needed, or contain so much that the relevant part is
crowded out. Tool descriptions may be poor, leading to the wrong tool or
the wrong inputs. Errors compound: a small misreading at step 3 shapes
every later decision, and the loop has no built-in way to notice that
its premise was wrong. An intermediate result may be accepted without
being checked. The loop may continue after it should have stopped, or
stop before the task was done. And a consequential action may be taken
that should have waited for approval.

Each failure has a counterpart in prevention, and none of the
counterparts is a property of the model alone: a clear task
specification with recognizable completion; tools with accurate
descriptions and bounded effects; observable checks built into the task
rather than assumed; permissions that make consequential actions wait;
and human review of the result. An agent system is as reliable as the
loop around the model, and the loop is where reliability is engineered.

## 13. Common misconceptions

**"The model itself ran the tool."** The model generated a structured
request. The surrounding software executed it, under its own rules, and
returned the result (§2).

**"Agent means fully autonomous."** An agent in this page's sense is a
system in which the model directs its sequence of actions within
constraints. Permission checks, stopping conditions, and the option to
ask the user are part of the design, and human approval can sit at any
step (§4, §10).

**"An agent is a different neural-network architecture."** It is not.
The model inside is an ordinary transformer language model. The agentic
behavior comes from the loop, the tools, the state, and the controls
around it (§5–§6).

**"Giving the agent a skill retrains it."** A skill, a project
instruction file, or any reusable procedure is loaded into inference-time
context. The parameters are unchanged (§8).

**"If the test passed, the task is correct."** A passing test is evidence
that the specified checks passed, and only that. It says nothing about
whether the specification was right or the checks were the right ones
(§9).

## 14. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>An agent's transcript shows the model writing "Running the test
suite now." What has actually happened at that point?</summary>
Only that the model produced that output. A test runs only if the model
also generated a structured tool request, the system's permission rules
allowed it, and the surrounding software executed it. The transcript
sentence by itself is output, not an action (§1–§2).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>What is the difference between a tool request and a tool
execution, and which does the model perform?</summary>
The model generates the request: structured output naming a tool and its
inputs. The surrounding system performs the external execution, after
checking permissions, and supplies the result to a subsequent model step
(§2).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>A system always runs the same three steps: extract the tables
from a report, check them against a database, write a summary. Is it a
workflow or an agent in this page's vocabulary?</summary>
A workflow. The sequence is predefined in code; the model fills in each
step but does not choose the steps. An agent would have meaningful
control over which steps and tools to use and in what order (§4).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>During a long task an agent writes notes to a file and reads
them back in later sessions. Which of the model's parameters, its context
window, or external state has changed?</summary>
Only external state. The file is persisted by the software and retrieved
into the context window of later calls. The parameters are untouched
(§7).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>All the automated checks an agent ran have passed. What can you
conclude?</summary>
That those checks passed. Whether the task specification was right, the
checks were the appropriate ones, or the overall result is correct
remains to be judged, by further checks or by a person (§9).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Why are permissions implemented in the software around the
model rather than relied on as a property of the model?</summary>
Because the software is what executes actions, so it is the only place a
boundary can be enforced regardless of what the model generates. A
well-behaved model reduces bad requests; it does not make a bad request
impossible, and it cannot stop an execution the software has already
allowed (§10).
</details>
:::

## 15. Continue learning

- **Anthropic, *Building Effective AI Agents*** (engineering article,
  published 2024-12-19). Practitioner level. The source of the
  workflow-versus-agent vocabulary used in §4, with a short catalogue of
  composable patterns and a clear statement of when not to build an
  agent. Limitation: one provider's engineering guidance, written for
  developers; terminology elsewhere differs.
  <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents>

- **Anthropic, *Tool use with Claude*** (API documentation page,
  accessed 2026-09-15). Practitioner level. A precise account of one
  provider's tool-call round trip: tool definitions, the structured
  request, execution by the developer's code, and the result returned.
  Limitation: product-specific and revised over time.
  <https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview>

- **Anthropic, *Claude Code* documentation: overview, skills, and
  permissions** (documentation pages, accessed 2026-09-15).
  Practitioner level. The concrete instances used in §8, §10, and §11.
  Limitation: product-specific; treat every detail as of the access
  date, and read the later practical pages of this course before relying
  on it.
  <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview>

See `resources.qmd` for the complete list of sources used across this
course, with full source-map entries.
